topics.title: SOC Architecture
topics.description: Understand how a Security Operations Center is structured

content.text: A Security Operations Center (SOC) is built on three fundamental pillars: People, Process, and Technology. Understanding how these elements work together is essential for effective security operations.
content.subtitle: The foundation of modern security operations

techBox.title: SOC Components
techBox.content:
People: Analysts, Engineers, Managers
Process: Workflows, Procedures, Playbooks
Technology: SIEM, EDR, NDR, Firewalls, IDS/IPS
Data: Logs, Alerts, Threat Intelligence

knowMore.title: Modern SOC Evolution
knowMore.content: Modern SOCs have evolved from simple monitoring centers to advanced threat hunting and incident response operations. Today's SOCs leverage automation, AI, and threat intelligence to stay ahead of sophisticated attacks.

steps.title: Centralization

steps.highlight: The SIEM acts as the central nervous system of the SOC

steps.description: Rules and analytics detect suspicious patterns
steps.highlight: Automated detection rules trigger when conditions are met

steps.title: Alert Generation
steps.description: Alerts are created and prioritized for analyst review
steps.highlight: Not all detections become alerts - filtering reduces noise

steps.highlight: This is where you come in as a SOC Analyst L1

demo.conclusion: Understanding this flow helps you see how your work fits into the bigger picture.

question.text: What are the three fundamental pillars of SOC architecture?
question.explanation: SOC architecture is built on three pillars: People (the analysts and teams), Process (the workflows and procedures), and Technology (the tools and systems used).

topics.title: Alerts & Events
topics.description: Learn the difference between events, alerts, incidents, and cases

content.text: Not everything that happens in your environment is a security incident. Understanding the hierarchy from events to cases is crucial for effective SOC operations.
content.subtitle: From raw data to actionable intelligence

techBox.title: The Security Hierarchy
techBox.content:
Event: Any recorded activity (login, file access, network connection)
Alert: An event that matches a detection rule
Incident: A confirmed security issue requiring response
Case: A documented investigation with evidence and actions

content.realWorldExample: Imagine your home security camera (events) detecting motion (alert). You investigate and confirm someone is actually breaking in (incident). You call the police and document everything that happened (case).

content.text: A typical enterprise generates millions of events per day, but only a small fraction become alerts. This filtering is essential to prevent analyst overwhelm.
content.subtitle: Why we don't investigate everything

techBox.title: Typical Volume Reduction
techBox.content:
Events per day: ~10,000,000
Alerts per day: ~10,000 (99.9% filtered)
Incidents per day: ~100 (99% are false positives)
Cases per day: ~10 (90% handled by L1)

question.text: Match each term to its correct definition:

pairs.right: Any recorded system or security activity
An event that matches a detection rule
A confirmed security issue requiring response

question.explanation: Understanding this hierarchy is fundamental to SOC operations. Events are raw data, alerts are filtered events, incidents are confirmed issues, and cases are formal investigations.

topics.title: Alert Triage
topics.description: Master the L1 analyst workflow for investigating alerts

content.text: Alert triage is the systematic process of investigating security alerts to determine if they represent real threats. As an L1 analyst, this is your primary responsibility.
content.subtitle: Your daily workflow as a SOC Analyst

techBox.title: The Standard Triage Workflow
techBox.content:
1. Understand the Alert - What detection rule triggered?
2. Identify the User - Who is involved?
3. Identify the Host - What system is affected?
4. Identify the IP - What network activity occurred?
5. Check Evidence - Review logs and telemetry
6. Make Decision - True positive, false positive, or escalate?

alert.title: Multiple Failed Login Attempts
alert.description: 10 failed login attempts detected for user Finance01 from IP 192.168.10.45

context.normalActivity: User typically logs in once per day between 8-9 AM

questions.question: What is the first thing you should check?
questions.feedback: Always start by understanding WHO is involved. Finance01 is Sarah Johnson, a Finance Manager.

questions.question: The failed logins happened at 2:32 PM. What does this tell you?
questions.feedback: Sarah normally logs in between 8-9 AM. Activity at 2:32 PM is unusual and worth investigating.

questions.question: What should you do next?
options: Check if there were any successful logins
Call IT to reboot the server
questions.correct: Check if there were any successful logins
questions.feedback: Correct! Check if any login succeeded after the failures. This could indicate a successful brute force attack.

content.text: Every alert investigation should answer specific questions. These questions guide your thinking and ensure you don't miss critical details.
content.subtitle: The analyst's mental checklist

techBox.title: The 5 W's of Alert Triage
techBox.content:
WHO: Which user/account is involved?
WHAT: What activity triggered the alert?
WHEN: When did this occur? Is timing suspicious?
WHERE: Which system/network location?
WHY: Why did the detection rule trigger?

question.text: Put these alert triage steps in the correct order:
question.explanation: The correct order ensures you systematically gather all necessary information before making a decision. Always understand what you're looking at first, then gather context about who and what is involved, review evidence, and finally make an informed decision.

topics.title: False Positives
topics.description: Learn to identify and handle false positive alerts

content.text: A false positive is an alert triggered by legitimate, authorized activity that matches a detection rule. Understanding false positives is crucial because they make up 90-95% of all alerts in a typical SOC.
content.subtitle: The most common challenge in SOC operations

techBox.title: Types of False Positives
techBox.content:
Expected Activity: Scheduled scans, backups, updates
Benign Activity: Normal business processes that look suspicious
Detection Errors: Rules that are too sensitive or poorly tuned
Legitimate Admin Activity: IT operations that trigger security alerts

content.realWorldExample: Your security system detects 'suspicious network scanning'. Investigation reveals it's the IT team's weekly vulnerability scanner - completely authorized and expected.

content.text: Experienced analysts develop pattern recognition for false positives. Here are key indicators that an alert might be a false positive.
content.subtitle: Signs you're looking at authorized activity

techBox.title: False Positive Indicators
techBox.content:
✓ Activity matches known scheduled tasks
✓ Source is an approved service account
✓ Occurs during maintenance windows
✓ Pattern matches normal business operations
✓ User confirms they performed the action
✓ Activity is part of documented process

knowMore.title: The Cost of False Positives
knowMore.content: High false positive rates lead to alert fatigue, where analysts become desensitized to alerts. This is dangerous because it increases the chance of missing real threats. Continuous tuning and feedback loops are essential to reduce false positives.

scenarios.details: Weekly vulnerability scan scheduled for Sundays at 2 AM
scenarios.explanation: This is expected, authorized activity from an approved scanner.

scenarios.alert: Multiple failed logins from external IP
scenarios.details: 100+ attempts from IP in Russia, user never logged in successfully
scenarios.explanation: External brute force attempt - definitely suspicious and requires investigation.

scenarios.details: User in Marketing uploaded 50GB to cloud storage at 3 PM
scenarios.explanation: Could be legitimate work, but unusual volume warrants verification with the user.

question.text: Which of these are indicators that an alert might be a false positive? (Select all that apply)
options: Activity matches a scheduled maintenance window
Source is from an unknown external IP
User confirms they performed the action
Activity involves a service account doing its job
Multiple users report similar alerts at the same time
correctAnswer: Activity matches a scheduled maintenance window
User confirms they performed the action
Activity involves a service account doing its job
question.explanation: Scheduled maintenance, user confirmation, and normal service account activity are all strong indicators of false positives. External IPs and multiple similar alerts could indicate real threats.

topics.title: Severity Classification
topics.description: Learn to assess and classify the severity of security incidents

content.text: Severity classification helps prioritize alerts and incidents. Not all security issues are equally urgent - proper classification ensures critical threats get immediate attention.
content.subtitle: Prioritizing your response

techBox.title: Standard Severity Levels
techBox.content:
CRITICAL: Active breach, data exfiltration, ransomware
HIGH: Successful compromise, privilege escalation, malware
MEDIUM: Suspicious activity, potential compromise, policy violations
LOW: Minor policy violations, informational alerts, false positives

content.text: Severity is determined by two factors: potential impact and confidence in the detection. A high-impact event with low confidence might be medium severity, while high impact + high confidence equals critical.
content.subtitle: The two dimensions of severity

techBox.title: Severity Calculation
techBox.content:
Impact: What damage could occur?
  - Data breach, system compromise, business disruption
Confidence: How sure are we this is real?
  - High: Clear evidence of malicious activity
  - Medium: Suspicious but needs verification
  - Low: Could be false positive

Severity = Impact × Confidence

scenarios.situation: Ransomware detected encrypting files on CEO's laptop
scenarios.evidence: High confidence - EDR confirmed ransomware signature
scenarios.explanation: Active ransomware on executive system = Maximum impact + High confidence = Critical severity. Immediate response required.

scenarios.evidence: User claims accidental click, immediately closed
scenarios.explanation: No malware downloaded, user aware and closed immediately. Low impact + benign explanation = Low severity.

scenarios.situation: Unusual outbound traffic to new domain
scenarios.evidence: Could be legitimate cloud service or C2 communication
scenarios.explanation: Potential data exfiltration (high impact) but uncertain if malicious (low confidence) = Medium severity. Requires investigation.

question.text: What two factors determine severity classification?
question.explanation: Severity is calculated based on the potential impact (how bad could this be?) and confidence (how sure are we this is real?). Both factors must be considered together.

topics.title: Escalation
topics.description: Know when and how to escalate incidents

content.text: Knowing when to escalate is just as important as knowing how to investigate. L1 analysts are the first line of defense, but not every incident should be handled at L1.
content.subtitle: When to ask for help

techBox.title: Escalation Tiers
techBox.content:
L1 Analyst: Triage, basic investigation, false positive identification
L2 Analyst: Deep investigation, correlation, IOC analysis
L3 / Senior Analyst: Threat hunting, advanced forensics, malware analysis
Specialist: Domain experts (network, endpoint, cloud, OT)
Management: Business impact decisions, external communications

content.text: Clear escalation criteria prevent both under-escalation (missing critical threats) and over-escalation (wasting senior analyst time). Here are the standard triggers.
content.subtitle: Escalation decision points

techBox.title: Escalate Immediately If:
techBox.content:
✓ Confirmed malware or ransomware
✓ Active data exfiltration
✓ Privilege escalation detected
✓ Critical system compromise
✓ Multiple related alerts (potential campaign)
✓ Unable to determine if true/false positive
✓ Involves executive or sensitive system
✓ Exceeds your investigation capability

knowMore.title: It's OK to Escalate
knowMore.content: New analysts sometimes hesitate to escalate, fearing they'll look inexperienced. The opposite is true - knowing your limits and escalating appropriately is a sign of good judgment. Seniors would rather investigate a false alarm than miss a real breach because an L1 analyst didn't escalate.

content.text: A good escalation provides all the context the next analyst needs to continue the investigation without starting from scratch. This saves time and ensures continuity.
content.subtitle: Writing effective escalation notes

techBox.title: Escalation Must Include:
techBox.content:
Summary: Brief description of the incident
Severity: Your assessed severity level
Evidence: Key findings and IOCs
Timeline: When did events occur?
Actions Taken: What you've already done
Recommendation: What you think should happen next
Urgency: Why this needs immediate attention

question.text: You've triaged an alert and confirmed malware on a user's laptop. The malware appears to be actively communicating with an external server. What should you do?
options: Close the alert - you identified the issue
Wait until tomorrow to see if it continues
question.explanation: Confirmed malware with active C2 communication is a clear escalation trigger. This requires immediate senior analyst attention for containment and further investigation.

topics.title: SOC Documentation
topics.description: Master the art of documenting security investigations

content.text: Documentation is not just paperwork - it's evidence, institutional knowledge, and legal protection. Your notes might be reviewed by lawyers, auditors, or investigators months or years later.
content.subtitle: Your investigation lives forever

techBox.title: Documentation Serves Multiple Purposes
techBox.content:
Legal: Court admissible evidence
Audit: Compliance and regulatory requirements
Knowledge: Training and process improvement
Communication: Handoffs between shifts/analysts
Metrics: Measuring SOC performance
Post-Incident: Learning from incidents

content.text: Complete documentation tells the story of your investigation from start to finish. Future analysts should be able to understand exactly what you did and why.
content.subtitle: The investigation narrative

techBox.title: Essential Documentation Elements
techBox.content:
Alert Details: What triggered the investigation
Timeline: Chronological sequence of events
Evidence: Logs, screenshots, IOCs collected
Actions Taken: Every step of your investigation
Findings: What you discovered
Conclusion: True/false positive, severity, disposition
Recommendations: Suggested next steps or improvements

demo.title: Documenting the FinCorp Investigation
demo.description: See how to document our earlier FinCorp failed login investigation

steps.title: Alert Information
steps.description: Start with what triggered the investigation
steps.highlight:
Alert: Multiple Failed Login Attempts
User: Finance01 (Sarah Johnson)
Host: FIN-PC-04
Time: 2024-01-15 14:32:18
Severity: Medium

steps.title: Investigation Summary
steps.highlight: Investigated alert for 10 failed login attempts to Finance01 account. Verified user identity, checked login patterns, and reviewed subsequent activity.

steps.title: Key Findings
steps.highlight:
1. Failed logins occurred outside normal business hours
2. Source IP 192.168.10.45 is user's assigned workstation
3. User contacted - confirmed she forgot password after returning from vacation
4. No successful logins after failed attempts
5. User reset password with IT at 14:45

steps.title: Evidence
steps.highlight:
Event ID 4625 (x10) from FIN-PC-04
User confirmation email
IT ticket #12345 for password reset

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.highlight: False Positive - Legitimate user forgot password. No malicious activity detected. Ticket closed.

demo.conclusion: This documentation tells the complete story. Anyone reading this ticket understands what happened and why you closed it.

content.text: Professional documentation is clear, concise, and objective. Follow these best practices to ensure your notes are useful and professional.
content.subtitle: Writing like a professional analyst

techBox.title: Documentation Guidelines
techBox.content:
DO:
✓ Use clear, professional language
✓ Document in real-time as you investigate
✓ Include timestamps
✓ Be specific (IP addresses, event IDs, etc.)
✓ State facts, not opinions

DON'T:
✗ Use slang or informal language
✗ Skip steps or assume things are obvious
✗ Forget to document negative findings
✗ Make assumptions without evidence
✗ Include personal opinions or speculation

question.text: Which of these should be included in incident documentation? (Select all that apply)
options: Your personal opinion about the user
Your guess about what might happen next
question.explanation: Professional documentation includes objective facts: timelines, evidence, actions, and fact-based conclusions. Personal opinions and speculation should not be included.
